questions.q: What are the three core discussion themes explicitly listed in the textbook's vH;kl (exercise) section for "dkys es?kk ikuh ns"?
questions.a: The three core discussion themes are: (1) Social hypocrisy and performative charity (vaèkfo'okl) — Question 1 asks about the basis of the name "Es<d&eaMyh" and why Banj Lsuk liked it; (2) Water as a survival right vs luxury — Question 3 asks why "ikuh ns, xqM+èkkuh ns" is demanded alongside water; (3) Systemic inequality and the narrator's complicity — Question 6 asks to analyze Thth's behavior toward Banj Lsuk in light of the story's message. A wrong answer listing generic themes like "poverty" or "water scarcity" without referencing the specific vH;kl questions reveals the student hasn't mapped textbook discussion prompts to oral preparation — they're preparing for written exams, not ASL.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the textbook includes the phrase "xxjh iwQVh cSy fi;klk" (the morning stars remain, the evenings remain) in the folk song refrain — what does this contrast with in the story's reality?
questions.a: The refrain "xxjh iwQVh cSy fi;klk" symbolizes nature's eternal, indifferent cycles — stars rise and set regardless of human suffering. This contrasts sharply with the story's reality where human-made systems (caste, class, municipal neglect) disrupt the natural right to water. The folk song's rhythm ("ikuh ns, xqM+èkkuh ns") carries collective resilience, while the narrative shows individualized desperation: Banj Lsuk begs door-to-door, Thth performs charity only when watched, and the colony's taps run dry while the privileged waste water. A student who only explains the literal meaning of "iwQVh" and "fi;klk" misses the ironic juxtaposition — the oral exam expects you to contrast the song's cosmic permanence with the story's social fragility.

questions.q: During a group discussion, a peer claims: "Thth is actually kind — he gives Banj Lsuk water eventually, and even gives her better food than his own family eats." Using ONLY textual evidence from the narrator's internal monologue, refute this claim in 90 seconds of spoken Hindi.
questions.a: (1) Point — Thth's kindness is performative and conditional, revealed by the narrator's own tongue-tied reluctance rather than by generosity, (2) Evidence one — he admits people were polite earlier yet resents her assertiveness to the very end, (3) Evidence two — what he separates out by hand for her is not better food but cattle feed, an act of dehumanisation, (4) Explanation — his charity is hypocrisy because he calculates that this will be called charity while denying her dignity, (5) Link — invoking the sages at the end to justify withholding proves the charity is self-serving theatre. A weak answer praises Thth's actions without reading what the narrator thinks, while oral analysis demands the internal monologue, not just the deeds.

questions.q: Compare how the folk song's collective voice ("dkys es?kk ikuh ns" — plural demand) differs from Thth's individualistic charity in addressing water justice. Which approach does the story endorse, and what textual evidence supports your conclusion?
questions.a: (1) The folk song's voice — plural imperatives demanding water and light, a community claiming resources as a right, (2) Thth's charity — individual, discretionary and hierarchical, measuring water out drop by drop onto the helpless girl, (3) The story's verdict — the ending shifts from his internal debate to systemic indictment, nights merging into nights while water drips drop by drop, implying structural failure rather than failed charity is the crisis, (4) Supporting evidence — the narrator's rhetorical question about the civilisational conscience growing callous implicates the entire social order. A student who answers that both approaches are needed misses the satirical thrust, since the author critiques charity as a distraction from justice.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement for an ASL discussion: "The story's ending — where Thth quotes sages to justify refusing water — proves that tradition and religion are the real enemies of social justice." Is this a fair reading of Parsai's intent? Defend your position with textual nuance.
questions.a: (1) Verdict — a reductive reading, because the target is the misuse of tradition rather than tradition itself, (2) The selective quote — Thth invokes the sages while ignoring their actual teaching that consistent giving accumulates the way drops of water collect in a vessel, (3) The deeper contrast — science and belief each have their own domain, and the ending asks whether educated people who act badly even without superstition deserve the same condemnation, (4) The fair reading — the satire indicts hypocrisy across both tradition and modernity, so declaring religion the enemy loses the textual nuance. A student who simplifies the satire this way loses marks for missing the dual critique.

questions.q: Create a 2-minute ASL-style spoken response to this prompt: "Imagine you are a resident of that colony 20 years later. The water crisis has worsened. Record a voice message for your colony WhatsApp group proposing ONE concrete collective action inspired by the story's folk song — not charity, but justice."
questions.a: (1) The opening — invoke the folk song's demand for water as a right rather than a song, (2) The diagnosis — people like Thth still hide behind charity to dodge their responsibility, so the failure is systemic, (3) The proposal — one concrete collective action, such as every household contributing a fixed monthly amount to a common water fund so the colony contracts tankers directly without depending on leaders or officials, (4) The closing — tie the community's unity to the song's enduring stars imagery and close with a meeting call of one voice and one right. A poor answer proposes vague awareness campaigns or petitioning the MLA, missing the story's lesson that collective self-reliance beats pleading with power.
